Appendix C. Cumulative impacts of mining and wind power development on reindeer: selection for grazing areas and movement at local scale (integrated step selection analysis)

Author

Bernardo B. Niebuhr, Erik Cronvall, Léonie Duris, Moudud Alam, Per Sandström, Anna Skarin

Here we describe the data and the results of the local assessment of reindeer habitat selection for grazing sites and movement patterns in the Malå reindeer herding community, Sweden, under the presence of mining and wind power development, for the three snow-free seasons: calving, summer, and autumn. The analysis consisted of a integrated step-selection analysis [iSSA; Avgar et al. (2016)] to simultaneously quantify effects on habitat selection at local scale and on movement parameters. We describe:

  • the reindeer GPS data used for the analyses;
  • how the analysis was set up;
  • the results of the iSSA models.

1 Goals of the analysis

The main question driving the iSSA analyses is: how is the selection of grazing sites by reindeer across seasons affected by wind power, mining, and other human infrastructure and activity, at a local scale? And how are movement parameters (movement rates and directionality) affected by the presence of wind turbines, during both construction and operation phases of the wind farms?

The specific questions are:

  • Are there cumulative impacts of multiple disturbance of the same type, e.g. multiple turbines or multiple wind parks? In other words, is there evidence of the impact of the density of wind turbines instead of only the nearest wind turibine?
  • Are there cumulative impacts of different types of disturbance, e.g. both wind power and mining?
  • What is the zone of influence of the impacts, i.e. up to which distance from disturbance is reindeer behavior altered?
  • How does the impacts change across seasons - calving, summer, and autumn?

2 Methods

2.1 Data

GPS data was collected by Sami reindeer herders through GPS collaring female reindeer between 2008 and 2018. No data was collected between 2012 and 2014, the years that followed the construction of the wind farm. Data was collected with a 2 hour fix rate, and failures or gaps were not considered for the analyses, and used to define the separation of the movement tracks into bursts. Data was only included in the analysis if there was at least forty consecutive days of movement data for each individual. Data was manually checked for all reindeer-years so that all positions representing reindeer being herd or GPS position of collars not attached to animals were removed. Furthermore, we used Bjørneraas et al (2010) procedure to remove spikes and outliers, and removed all locations found within known fenced areas and corrals, which are typically used for reindeer handling.

The iSSA was based on data of 218 reindeer tracked during calving, 200 reindeer tracked during summer, and 176 reindeer tracked during autumn. Table C1 shows the number of individuals and number of used GPS positions recorded in each year.

Table C1. Number of reindeer monitored (number of GPS positions recorded, in parenthesis) in each year and season.

2.2 Statistical modeling

To assess the impact of mining, wind turbines, and other infrastructure on reindeer habitat selection at local scale and reindeer movement, we performed integrated step selection analyses [iSSA; Avgar et al. (2016)]. iSSA is designed to quantify simultaneaously the effects of the covariates on habitat selection and movement, while controlling for each other’s mutual influence. In iSSA, the unit of analysis is the step or displacement made by reindeer between subsequent positions - here, 2 h from each other. Similarly to resource selection analyses, the data in put into a use-availability design. For each used step, we sampled 10 random steps starting in the same position. Step length and angle for the random steps were drawn from a Gamma distribution and a von Mises distribution fitted to the step lengths and turning angles for each individual, respectively. Random steps leaving the limits of the availability area in each season were excluded and redrawn. For each step, we extracted the environmental covariates at the end point of steps to assess habitat selection, and at the starting point of steps to assess effects on movement parameters.

We prepared the data and performed the iSSA using the tools from the amt package in R (Signer, Fieberg, and Avgar 2019) and followed the interpretation of parameters according to Fieberg et al. (2021). Models were fitted using conditional logistic regression through the function amt::issf(). They considered use/availability as a response variable, the step id as the strata, and the effects of wind power, mining, and other infrastructure (private and public roads, power lines, houses, trails) as covariates. We also added other land cover and phenology related variables - elevation, slope, aspect, terrain position index (TPI), and date of the start of the season (SOS) (or end of season, EOS, for autumn). TPI is a measure of variation in the relief of a neighborhood, computed by comparing the elevation of a site with the average elevation on the neighborhood, for a given neighborhood size/scale (De Reu et al. 2013). Here the TPI was computed using neighborhoods of different sizes (150 m, 250 m, and 510 m) and the best TPI scale was defined through model selection (see below). SOS and EOS are phenological variables based on NDVI that show the time of peak greening and browning of the vegetation in spring and autumn (Kong et al. 2022). Given our questions, our focus was mainly on estimating the impacts of wind power and mining, so the other variables were mainly included to control for their possible, additive effects. All variables that were not in log scale were standardized to mean 0 and variance 1, to facilitate convergence of the model fits.

We assessed if and how the impacts of wind power and mining accumulated using the approach from Niebuhr et al. (2023). To represent the spatial influence of wind power and mining, we computed zones of influence (ZOI) that decayed exponentially from the disturbance source and vanished at varying distances, from 100 m to 10 km. For wind power, we computed both the density of wind turbines (representing the cumulative impact of multiple turbines) and the ZOI of the nearest feature (see the main text for details); for mining we only considered the ZOI of the nearest mine, since there is only one main mining site in the study area. For simplicity, the influence of all other infrastructure types was modeled using the log-distance to the nearest feature. To evaluate the impact of wind farms in a before-after setup, comparing the movement behavior of reindeer before, during, and after the construction of the wind farms, we created two variables to represent the influence of wind farms: wind_ZOI_construction and wind_ZOI_operation. Each of them assumed the value of the ZOI only during the construction and operation phases, respectively, and were zero otherwise. This means that they represented the effect of the wind turbines in the different phases, compared to the period before the construction, when the wind turbines were not present.

The overall model structure we fitted was the following:

base_formula <- case_ ~ strata(step_id_) +
  # movement
  sl_ + log_sl + cos_ta +
  wind_turbines_YYY_start_construction_scaled:(sl_ + log_sl + cos_ta) +
  wind_turbines_ZZZ_start_operation_scaled:(sl_ + log_sl + cos_ta) +
  landcover_cc_grouped_start:(sl_ + log_sl + cos_ta) +
  # habitat selection
  dem_end_scaled + I(dem_end_scaled^2) + slope_end_scaled +
  sos_end_scaled +
  log_power_lines_dist_end + log_priv_road_dist_end + log_public_road_dist_end +
  log_house_dist_end + 
  landcover_cc_grouped_end +
  # minig habitat selection
  mining_Krist_nearestXXX_end_scaled + 
  # wind habitat selection
  wf_name_end +
  wind_turbines_YYY_end_construction_scaled +
  wind_turbines_ZZZ_end_operation_scaled +
  landcover_cc_grouped_end:wind_turbines_YYY_end_construction_scaled +
  landcover_cc_grouped_end:wind_turbines_ZZZ_end_operation_scaled +
  # tpi habitat selection
  tpi_scale_TTT

where case_ is our response variable, sl_, log_sl and cos_ta are the movement parameters (step length, log(step length), and cosine of the turning angle, respectively). This structure contains the movement parameters, including the effects of land cover and wind turbines; habitat selection considering the effects of wind turbines in each phase (construction, operation) in interaction with land cover; and main effects of other infrastructure and landscape variables. The terms start and end refer to variables extracted at the start or end points of a step; dem refers to elevation, and wf_name refers to the name of the closest wind farm to each point, added as a fixed effect to control for differential effects close to the Åmliden wind park, which lies along a large fenced area.

The terms XXX, YYY, ZZZ, and TTT in the model structure above represent scales or variables that varied across models fitted. To evaluate the most likely ZOI for the mine and the wind turbines, whether there was a cumulative impact of multiple wind farms, and at which scale the TPI most affected reindeer habitat selection and movement, we replaced these variables in the model structure above using each possible combination of ZOI radii and type (cumulative vs. nearest) for wind power and the different ZOI radii for mining, together with different scales for the TPI. Models were compared through the Akaike information criterion (AIC), and the most parsimonious model was selected as the one with smaller AIC (Burnham and Anderson 2002).

To interpret the results, we first checked the structure of the best ranking models (through the AIC and their difference; we considered models different if \(\Delta AIC\) > 2; Burnham and Anderson 2002) and compared how they differed qualitatively. Second, we evaluated the coefficients of the best ranked model for each season. Third, for habitat selection, we plotted the relative selection strength [RSS; Avgar et al. (2017)] (or the log (RSS)) for wind turbines and land cover, as well as for mining. Finally, for movement patterns, we plotted the differences in movement rates and turning angles for movements close (distance = 0) and far (distance = 1 and 5 km) from the wind turbines, in each phase (construction/operation). We only plotted results when there was a significant effect.

3 Results

3.1 Model selection

Summary of best ranked models:

  • Calving. Cumulative impact of wind turbines, ZOI radius = 5 km; log-distance effect of the mine:

3.1.1 Calving

Table C2 shows the ranking of most parsimonious model for iSSA during calving. The best model for calving included the additive effect of the log-distance to the mine and the cumulative zone of influence wind turbines at 5 km radius (Table C2). The six models following in the ranking all give support to the a cumulative effect of wind turbines at 5 km and a TPI of 150 m, but the ZOI of the mine for these models is vary variable, from 250 m to 10km. This supports the expectation of a cumulative impact of wind turbines on habitat selection and movement, but points to limited impact of the mine on habitat selection at local scale.

Table C2. Table of model selection for the iSSA models for calving. Columns are zone of influence (ZOI) radius for mining and wind turbines, scale for the terrain position index (TPI), AIC of the model, dAIC of each model in relation to the most parsimonious model, and the formula with each model’s structure. Variables with ‘Log’ correspond to the log-distance to the nearest feature for that variable. For impact of wind turbines, cumulative represents the density of turbines, and nearest represents the distance-decay ZOI of the nearest turbine.

3.1.2 Summer

Table C3 shows the ranking of most parsimonious model for iSSA during summer. The best model for summer included the additive effect of the ZOI to the mine with 10 km radius and ZOI of the nearest wind turbine at 5 km radius (Table C3). However, other models with ZOI of 5 km for the mine and 10 km for wind turbines are equally plausible (dAIC < 2). To be conservative and not assume a too large zone of influence, we consider for the results the model with ZOI of mine with radius 5 km, and an additive effect of the nearest wind turbine at 5 km.
This result refutes the expectation of cumulative impact of the turbines, but supports the expectation of an additive impact of both mining and wind farms at large scales (5 km) on local habitat selection and movement.

Table C3. Table of model selection for the iSSA models for summer. Columns are zone of influence (ZOI) radius for mining and wind turbines, scale for the terrain position index (TPI), AIC of the model, dAIC of each model in relation to the most parsimonious model, and the formula with each model’s structure. Variables with ‘Log’ correspond to the log-distance to the nearest feature for that variable. For impact of wind turbines, cumulative represents the density of turbines, and nearest represents the distance-decay ZOI of the nearest turbine.

3.1.3 Autumn

Table C4 shows the ranking of most parsimonious model for iSSA during autumn. The best model for autumn included the additive effect of the log-distance to the mine and the cumulative ZOI of wind turbines with 10 km radius (Table C4). All the best ranked models (dAIC < 2) present the cumulative ZOI of wind turbines with 10 km and TPI at 510 m, giving evidence of a large-scale, cumulative impact of wind turbines on local habitat selection and movement in autumn. In contrast, the same models present widely varying ZOI radius for the mine, pointing to no effect of the mine on local habitat selection in autumn.

Table C4. Table of model selection for the iSSA models for autumn. Columns are zone of influence (ZOI) radius for mining and wind turbines, scale for the terrain position index (TPI), AIC of the model, dAIC of each model in relation to the most parsimonious model, and the formula with each model’s structure. Variables with ‘Log’ correspond to the log-distance to the nearest feature for that variable. For impact of wind turbines, cumulative represents the density of turbines, and nearest represents the distance-decay ZOI of the nearest turbine.

3.2 Disturbance effects on step selection

Here we present the coefficients of the iSSA models on the habitat selection. Even though all results come from the same models, we split the way we present the parts of the resulting model, to ease its interpretation. In this section we restrict ourselves on presenting the coefficients of all infrastructure and landscape covariates, without going into details regarding the impact of wind farms on habitat selection and on movement patterns. These results are shown in details in the following sections.

3.2.1 Coefficients for other infrastructure - All seasons

Here we show the coefficient estimates for all the infrastructure types, excluding wind turbines. The estimates are put together for the different seasons in table C5 so it is easy to compare the effects between them.

A summary of the results:

  • The mine was avoided in calving and summer, but not during autumn;
  • Public and private roads were avoided in all seasons;
  • There was no effect of power lines in calving and summer, and a slight selection for them during autumn;
  • Houses were selected during calving and autumn (why??);
  • Start of season did not affect habitat selection during calving and summer; however, end of season was positively selected in autumn, which means animals select for areas which stay green longer in autumn.

Table C5. Coefficient estimates for the effects of infrastructure types and the start/end of season on habitat selection for all three seasons.

3.3 Impacts of mining and wind turbine on step selection

Here we plot, for each season, the effect of the mine and the wind turbines, while keeping all the other variables at their median values, to illustrate the mean effect of these two types of infrastructure.

3.3.1 Calving

The mine in Kristeneberget was strongly avoided during calving, according to the iSSA (Fig. C1). It is not possible to objectively set a ZOI for the mine because the the best variable representing its impact was the log-distance to the mine (instead one of the ZOI distance-decay curves that better define the ZOI radius). However, interpreting qualitatively the curve in Fig. C1 and assessing the second best-ranked model in Table C2, we can say the ZOI radius of the mine at local level in calving is at least 250 m, but possibly larger.

In calving and during the construction of the wind farms, local habitat selection was affected by the density of wind turbines at 5 km ZOI. This means there was evidence of cumulative impacts of multiple wind turbines/farms on reindeer responses. Figure C2 illustrates that. The upper panel shows the expected response curves (the log Relative selection strength) as reindeer gets away from wind turbines, if hypothetically there was only one turbine. In this case, the impact would be small. However, the impact increases as the density of turbines increase (Fig. C2; n = 10 in the bottom panels), and turbines are significantly avoided within coniferous forests and marginally avoided in open areas.

During operation, the responses are qualitatively similar to the construction phase, but they are not significant, as it is shown in Fig. C3.

3.3.2 Summer

During summer, the mine was avoided at local scale. Even though the identified ZOI radius was 5 km, the effect size was small so the response curve of the effect of the mine decreases very fast from its maximum effect near the turbines (Fig. C4).

During summer, there was no evidence of cumulative impacts of multiple wind farms at local scale, but there was an effect of the nearest wind turbine with ZOI radius of 5 km. Areas closer to the wind turbines were selected in open lands, coniferous forests and mires, compared to deciduous forests, mostly during construction phase (Fig. C5).

3.3.3 Autumn

There was no effect of the mine at local scale habitat selection during autumn (p > 0.05, Table C8). The wind farms did not significantly affect reindeer local-scale habitat selection either (Table C8, Fig. C6).

3.4 Impacts of wind turbines on movement patterns

Here we present the coefficients for the movement parameters included in the iSSA, i.e. all term involving step lengths and turning angles.

3.4.1 Coefficients - Calving

Table C9 shows the coefficient estimates of the iSSA model for the variables affecting the movement parameters and is complementary to table C6.

Table C9. Coefficient estimates for calving for the movement parameters within the iSSA.

During calving, there was an effect of wind turbines during the construction period, with a cumulative impact of multiple wind turbines and ZOI radius of 5 km. This led to increased movement rates and more directional movements when reindeer were close to the location of the wind farms, compared to places far away from them. During the operation period, though, this effect was not present.

3.4.2 Coefficients - Summer

There were no detectable results of the wind turbines on the movement parameters during summer, as shown in Table C10.

Table C10. Coefficient estimates for summer for the movement parameters within the iSSA.

3.4.3 Coefficients - Autumn

There were no detectable results of the wind turbines on the movement parameters during autumn, as shown in Table C11.

Table C11. Coefficient estimates for autumn for the movement parameters within the iSSA.
